blogs.title: Algorithmic Adjudication: How *Williams v. GoAuto* Validates Automated Contract Termination Under Louisiana's 'Strict Adherence' Standard
blogs.description: This post analyzes the tension between Louisiana's longstanding requirement of 'strict adherence' to insurance cancellation statutes and the Fifth Circuit's approval of a fully automated, pre-signature cancellation process. It explores how the court reconciled the statutory mandate for human-like procedural safeguards with a reality where computer systems effectuate cancellations milliseconds after receiving an email, effectively ruling that 'receipt' occurs at the server level rather than upon human review or physical possession.

blogs.title: The Semantics of Certification: Why the Fifth Circuit Refused to Read a Signature Requirement Into La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550
blogs.description: Focusing on statutory interpretation, this article examines the court's refusal to imply a signature requirement where the text only demands a 'statement certifying' compliance. The post contrasts the Fifth Circuit's textualist approach with the plaintiffs' reliance on *Benitez v. Elsayed*, discussing the broader implications for corporate liability when entities use standardized, unsigned digital certifications versus individualized, signed affidavits in regulated industries.

blogs.title: Defining Digital 'Receipt': Possession, Custody, and the Obsolescence of Physical Delivery in Insurance Law
blogs.description: This entry dives into the court's redefinition of 'receipt' under Black's Law Dictionary for the digital age. By determining that an insurer takes 'possession' of a cancellation request the moment its API accepts data from a finance company's system—regardless of whether a human employee has touched the document—the opinion signals a major shift in how courts view constructive notice and delivery in paperless commercial transactions, potentially rendering older precedents regarding physical filing cabinets and private carriers obsolete.

blogs.title: The High Bar for Certification: Why Unsettled State Law Isn't Enough to Invoke Federal Question Certification
blogs.description: Analyzing the procedural posture of the case, this post critiques the plaintiffs' failed attempt to certify questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court. It reviews the Fifth Circuit's application of the *Jefferson* standard, highlighting how federal appellate courts balance the importance of novel state law issues against the scarcity of certification resources, and what this denial suggests about the threshold required for federal courts to defer complex state statutory interpretations to state high courts.
